title: P versus RP
formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\)? In other words, can randomness be removed from every polynomial-time decision algorithm that never accepts a false instance and accepts each true instance with probability at least one half?

Let \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be any language for which there is one probabilistic Turing machine \(A\), with a polynomial worst-case time bound on every random tape, such that
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]\ge\tfrac12,\qquad x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[A(x)=1]=0.\]
Must there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(D\) and constants \(C>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[D(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)\qquad\text{within }C(|x|+1)^a\text{ steps}?\]
The machine and constants may depend on the language, but not on its particular input.
why: This is a central question about whether random choices enlarge efficient decision power even when false acceptances are forbidden. It tests a basic source of randomized algorithmic speed and connects the construction of deterministic algorithms with strong circuit lower bounds and the broader boundary between finding and verifying solutions.
status_note: Source-open in Vadhan’s 2012 monograph, Open Problem 2.10. On 16 September 2026 this review checked Definitions 2.8–2.13, the ordinary-language versus promise distinctions and the conditional 1997 hardness-versus-randomness theorem. A bounded later-work search found no verified unconditional equality or separation. Lin’s arXiv:2308.09549v9 (19 July 2026) claims a separation, but its Theorem 4.2 allows an exponent depending on the encoded input machine, while Theorem 6.2 infers RP membership from an increasing union of fixed-exponent RP languages. That inference is invalid and supplies no uniform polynomial bound for the whole language. The claim is therefore not treated as a resolution. This is a bounded source and claim assessment, not an exhaustive literature certification or a new Lean proof.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that a language in \(\mathrm E\) with exponential Boolean-circuit complexity implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\), which would in particular imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\).
Vadhan explicitly retains P versus RP as Open Problem 2.10 and distinguishes it from the two-sided-error and promise-problem comparisons.

importance.reason: A defining derandomization question for a standard complexity class, with consequences for all one-sided-error polynomial-time algorithms. Its scope and asymmetric relationship with P versus NP justify a separate landmark card alongside the stronger P versus BPP question.

sentences: RP consists of languages decided in worst-case polynomial time using fair random bits, with no false acceptances.
The question asks whether every such language also has a uniform deterministic polynomial-time decider.
Each language may have its own fixed polynomial bound, but the exponent cannot vary with the input.
Strong circuit-hardness assumptions imply derandomization, while deterministic algorithms for individual examples do not settle the whole class comparison.
A resolution would determine whether one-sided-error randomness increases efficient decision power.

definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings, including the possible empty string. The indicator \(\mathbf1_L(x)\) is one when \(x\in L\) and zero otherwise. A decision algorithm must terminate with one of these two answers on every input; there is no promise excluding some binary strings from its correctness requirement. Input length \(n=|x|\) is the full number of input bits.

Use classical multitape Turing machines with a fixed finite alphabet and finite transition description. Polynomial time means that there are an integer \(a\ge0\) and a constant \(C\ge1\) for which the running time is at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every input of length \(n\). All bit operations and all random-bit requests take time. Uniformity means that one finite machine works at every input length. No advice string depending on \(n\), oracle, quantum operation or real-number register is supplied.

The class \(\mathrm P\) contains exactly the languages decided correctly by deterministic polynomial-time machines. A probabilistic machine additionally obtains independent fair random bits during its execution. It has a polynomial time bound on every input and every sequence of random choices, not merely in expectation or with high probability. Thus only polynomially many random bits can be read. Shorter random computations may be padded with ignored bits without changing their acceptance probabilities.

More explicitly, the probabilistic definition can be written using a deterministic machine \(A(x,r)\), a polynomially bounded integer function \(p(n)\), and a uniform string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\). The machine runs in time polynomial in \(n\) for all such pairs, and unused bits of \(r\) are ignored. Each tape \(r\) has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). The probability in the statement is over this finite sample space separately for each fixed \(x\); it is not an average over an input distribution. The function \(p\) is computable in polynomial time and may be taken to be an integer-coefficient polynomial bound by padding.

The class \(\mathrm{RP}\) consists of languages satisfying the two displayed probability conditions. A no-instance has no accepting random tape. A yes-instance has accepting tapes occupying at least half the sample space. The machine may reject some yes-instances on unlucky tapes; it never accepts a no-instance. Replacing the acceptance threshold one half by another fixed constant strictly between zero and one gives the same class. An arbitrarily small positive acceptance probability, without an inverse-polynomial lower bound, does not give this definition.

The deterministic inclusion \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{RP}\) follows by ignoring randomness. The question is therefore whether \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm P\). Equality requires a deterministic polynomial-time decider for every language in \(\mathrm{RP}\). A negative answer requires some language \(L\in\mathrm{RP}\) for which no deterministic decider has any polynomial worst-case time bound. The negative claim must quantify over all deterministic machines and all fixed polynomial exponents; it is not a separation at one selected exponent.

The deterministic polynomial exponent may depend on the language or on a chosen randomized decider for it. It may not depend on the particular input. In particular, a construction that handles each encoded randomized or deterministic machine within a time whose exponent is encoded in the input need not have one polynomial bound. Nor does showing that a language is an increasing union of polynomial-time languages put that union in polynomial time. The target is a single machine with a single polynomial bound for each whole language.

Equality of these language classes does not require a computable compiler that takes every description of an RP machine and produces a deterministic simulation. A proved universal transformation would be sufficient, but the acceptance criterion is the class inclusion itself. The deterministic machine need only decide membership; it need not reproduce the randomized machine’s output distribution, internal choices or running-time exponent.

For comparisons, \(\mathrm{coRP}\) consists of the complements of RP languages. Its machines always accept yes-instances and accept a no-instance with probability at most one half. Since deterministic polynomial time is closed under complementation, \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{coRP}\). The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) permits two-sided error: yes-instances are accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and no-instances with probability at most \(1/3\), with the same worst-case polynomial time convention. The stronger equality \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\) would imply the equality asked here; the card does not replace one-sided error by two-sided error.

A promise problem specifies disjoint sets of yes-instances and no-instances and imposes correctness only on their union. Derandomizing all promise versions of RP is a separately quantified stronger task. The promise-class implication connecting one-sided and two-sided derandomization must not be presented as an equivalence of the ordinary language equalities without further justification.

For another comparison, \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. An accepting random tape is a certificate, so \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\), whereas \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{RP}\) would imply \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The positive answer to this card does not itself assert that every NP language has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

The conditional result in the progress section uses \(\mathrm E=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{cn})\). An exponential circuit lower bound there means that some language in \(\mathrm E\) and some constant \(\alpha>0\) require Boolean circuits of size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large input length \(n\). Circuits use the fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, with size measured by gates; they may differ freely with \(n\). This circuit-hardness assumption is background for a conditional theorem, not an assumption of the question.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{RP}\subseteq\mathrm P\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language belongs to \(\mathrm{RP}\) and not to \(\mathrm P\), with the machines, probability conventions and uniform worst-case time bounds specified here. Equality must cover all RP languages; a deterministic algorithm for only one example does not suffice without a proved reduction covering the entire class. A separation must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time decider, not just a proposed simulation or one polynomial exponent. Conditional derandomization, nonuniform circuits, oracle separations, average-input guarantees and correctness at only infinitely many input lengths do not settle the unconditional language comparison. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this exact class-equality target.

source_formulation.text: Vadhan’s Open Problem 2.10 asks whether P equals RP immediately after defining one-sided-error randomized polynomial time. This card retains that ordinary language-class equality and its worst-case time convention.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Problem 2.10; no change of mathematical target

context_blocks.text: An RP computation has a useful asymmetry: any observed acceptance is trustworthy, yet an observed rejection may be a missed opportunity to accept. A substantial fraction of random choices succeeds on each yes-instance. The question asks whether that availability of successful choices always translates into deterministic polynomial-time decision.

Repeating the randomized algorithm can make its failure probability very small, while retaining a polynomial running time. This reduces error but still uses randomness. Likewise, the existence of good advice for each input length does not by itself give one uniform deterministic algorithm.

Polynomial identity testing is a representative algebraic example. Given an arithmetic circuit, it asks whether the computed polynomial is identically zero. Vadhan’s Theorem 2.12 places identity testing over the integers in coRP, and therefore its nonidentity complement in RP. A deterministic identity test would be a substantial special-case advance, but no completeness equivalence with all RP languages is assumed.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove that exponential circuit hardness for a language in \(\mathrm E\) implies \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\), and hence \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{RP}\). This connects removing random choices to proving strong computational lower bounds. The hardness premise remains an assumption of that theorem.

The logical relation to P versus NP is asymmetric. A deterministic solution of every NP language would also cover RP, while a proved RP separation would give an NP separation. An equality between P and RP can still leave open the possibility of harder NP languages whose accepting certificates are too sparse to be found by the original random-tape guarantee.

Derandomization for restricted algebraic computations, special graph problems, shorter random tapes or promise classes concerns useful neighboring questions. This card asks for the entire uniform language class with one-sided error, without an input distribution or a special form of algorithm.
